newsitem.title: USA: U.S. groups make clean air top Earth Day topic.
newsitem.headline: U.S. groups make clean air top Earth Day topic.

text.p: Earth Day, in some years an occasion for raucous demonstrations for the environmental movement, is expected to pass without noisy fanfare on Tuesday in events across the nation.

The focus of the 27th Earth Day will be on local activities -- concerts, speeches, park cleanups, tree-plantings. Much activity will center on promoting the Clinton administration's proposal to strengthen air quality standards that has sparked an uproar among industries.

"This year we're focusing more on targeted protests. It's not every year that we look to draw 150,000 people to the Mall (in Washington)," Daniel Rosenberg, staff attorney for the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, said.
For the last two years, environmental groups rallied on Earth Day to fight attempts by the Republican-led Congress to ease environmental regulations for businesses and industries.
Most of those efforts failed, and the new Republican-led Congress said it intended to be far greener.

"Certainly the intensity and the scale of the attack is less, but we see the attacks are there and as serious as ever," Rosenberg said. "The Clean Air Act is evidence, and that's what we're focusing on."

"Last year's Earth Day was more focused on the negative. It was a defensive Earth Day, and this year is more of a positive agenda and the clean air regulations are the centerpiece of that," Carl Pope, executive director of the Sierra Club, said.
The Environmental Protection Agency, directed by the Clean Air Act to review health standards for major air pollutants every five years, has proposed stiffer new standards against smog and soot.

The proposal has sparked a lobbying frenzy by industry groups who say it would cost them billions of dollars and by environmental and health groups who say it would greatly improve the nation's health and extend thousands of lives.
The administration is expected to announce a final decision on the rule in July, but Congress then could review the rule and, if there is a two-third majority, overturn it.
While the air standards fight is stirring some Earth Day enthusiasm, environmental advocates said the calendar worked against promoting a major hoopla this year.

"Historically Earth Day is a cyclical thing. This year it's on Passover, it's a Tuesday, and there's not a big rallying focus like a threat from the 105th Congress. But you still see a lot interest where it counts, in schools and local actions across the country," Greg Wetstone, the Natural Resources Defense Council's legislative director, said.
